meta.description: Voltaire, closing a verse epistle to Émilie du Châtelet. It is a quatrain, not a sentence — and the French says ‘lovable,’ not ‘loved.’
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'One dies twice, I see it plainly'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Voltaire: the last four lines of his epistle to Émilie du Châtelet, in print by 1743. Here’s the French, and the word the English drops.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: These are the closing four lines of Voltaire’s verse epistle to Émilie du Châtelet, the one that begins ‘Si vous voulez que j’aime encore.’ Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest printing to the Paris journal Mercure de France in 1743, in a slightly different version, with the familiar text following in the 1745 collected works.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Épître à Madame du Châtelet (‘Si vous voulez que j’aime encore’)
Verse epistle — these are its last four lines
Volume VI of the collected works, 1745

source.excerpt:
On meurt deux fois, je le vois bien:
Cesser d’aimer et d’être aimable,
C’est une mort insupportable;
Cesser de vivre, ce n’est rien.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ gives the tracing: a variant in the Mercure de France in 1743, then the settled text in volume VI of a large collection of Voltaire’s works in 1745.
The quatrain closes the epistle to Émilie du Châtelet reproduced in Voltaire’s correspondence for 1741 at French Wikisource ↗ — the poem circulated in a letter before it reached print.

Both the printed sources and the manuscript trail run through du Châtelet, Voltaire’s companion and intellectual partner of sixteen years, which is what fixes the poem’s subject as well as its author.
source.excerptNote: The popular English says ‘to cease to love and be loved.’ Voltaire wrote cesser d’aimer et d’être aimable — to cease to love and to be lovable. The difference is the whole point: he is writing about ageing out of the capacity to attract, not about losing someone’s affection. No single translator owns the English wording; it circulates as a prose rendering of a quatrain.
source.rightsNote: Public domain. The French verse was in print by 1743 and Voltaire died in 1778; nothing here is anywhere near copyright.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: About Voltaire
author.bio: Voltaire — pen name of François-Marie Arouet — is remembered for the satire and the polemics, which makes the love poetry easy to miss. He spent the 1730s and 1740s at Cirey with Émilie du Châtelet, the physicist who translated Newton’s Principia into French; by the time he wrote this epistle he was in his late forties and their affair had cooled into something else. The quatrain is what he made of that.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The epistle opens by asking Émilie du Châtelet to give him back the age of love if she wants him to go on loving — and then, over the length of the poem, gives that up and settles for friendship instead. The quatrain is the concession at the end. Voltaire is in his forties, well aware that the passion has run out and that what remains is affection and work.

What makes the four lines land is the ranking. He is not saying that love matters more than survival in some sentimental way; he is saying, flatly and with the shrug of ‘je le vois bien,’ that he has already been through the worse of the two deaths and found the other one negligible by comparison.
detailsBody: Être aimable is not ‘to be loved.’ It means to be lovable — attractive, worth loving. Voltaire is describing the moment a person stops being someone others could fall for, which is a fact about ageing rather than about a relationship ending. English translations almost always flatten it to ‘be loved,’ which turns a poem about growing old into a poem about being left.

The dating is layered rather than uncertain. The verse circulated in manuscript and in Voltaire’s correspondence — French Wikisource files the epistle under 1741 — before Quote Investigator’s earliest printed appearance in the Mercure de France in 1743, with the familiar wording arriving in the 1745 collected works. This page cites the print record because that is what can be checked.
context.pull: He is not ranking love above life for effect. He has already been through the first death and found the second one negligible.
